planting.note: Set container-grown grafted trees out after the last frost in a sheltered, south-facing spot, since this is one of the more cold-hardy true citrus species.

directions: Tachibana is the only citrus believed truly native and wild to Japan, long valued more for its fragrant white spring flowers and cultural symbolism than for eating fresh, since the small round fruits are intensely sour and seedy. Grow it as a small evergreen tree in full sun with sharply drained soil, and protect it the first few winters until the woody framework matures, as it tolerates more cold than most mandarin-type citrus once established. The tart juice and zest are traditionally used in regional condiments and teas rather than eaten out of hand. Light annual pruning keeps the dense twiggy canopy open and encourages the heavy flowering it is prized for.
sources: University of California Riverside Citrus Variety Collection
Japan Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries citrus germplasm records

planting.note: Transplant grafted stock after frost danger passes into full sun with excellent drainage; fruit matures slowly and is typically picked in midwinter.

directions: First discovered on Innoshima Island in Hiroshima Prefecture, hassaku produces medium-large, thick-rinded pale yellow fruit with a distinctive firm, slightly chewy segment texture and a pleasant mild bitterness balancing its sweetness. Plant it like other subtropical mandarin-type citrus in full sun with regular but not soggy irrigation, and expect the fruit to hang on the tree into winter before reaching peak eating quality in January and February. Because the peel clings tightly to the flesh, it is usually peeled with a knife rather than by hand. It makes a handsome dooryard tree with glossy evergreen foliage and fragrant spring bloom.
sources: University of California Riverside Citrus Variety Collection
Japan Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries citrus germplasm records

planting.note: Plant after frost danger into full sun; this is a true overwintering citrus left on the tree through winter and harvested the following spring.

directions: Natsudaidai is unusual among citrus for ripening in autumn yet being deliberately left hanging on the tree all winter, with harvest delayed until spring or early summer once the fruit's sharp acidity has mellowed somewhat, which is how it earned its name meaning 'summer daidai orange.' The grapefruit-sized yellow fruit still carries a pronounced tart-bitter edge even at full maturity, so it is used mainly for marmalade, zest, and flavoring rather than fresh eating. Give it the same full-sun, well-drained conditions and winter protection as other subtropical Japanese citrus, and expect a vigorous, upright tree that needs a long growing season to size up its large fruit. It is a parent of several sweeter modern Japanese citrus selections.
sources: University of California Riverside Citrus Variety Collection
Japan Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries citrus germplasm records

planting.note: Plant grafted trees after frost danger in full sun; fruit can be left to hang into late winter and spring before picking.

directions: This naturally occurring sweeter bud mutation of natsudaidai was found in Oita Prefecture and has largely replaced the sharper-tasting original in Japanese orchards because its large yellow fruit keeps the same striking size while losing much of the harsh bitterness. Grow and train it exactly like standard natsudaidai, in full sun with consistent moisture during fruit development and some winter protection in marginal climates. Fruit still benefits from hanging on the tree well past ripening color change before picking, which rounds out the flavor further. It is a good choice for gardeners who want the dramatic look of natsudaidai with easier fresh eating.
sources: University of California Riverside Citrus Variety Collection
Japan Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries citrus germplasm records

planting.note: Transplant after last frost into full sun; harvest runs midwinter and fruit holds well on the tree for an extended picking window.

directions: Named for the historic Iyo Province now part of Ehime Prefecture, where it is grown commercially on a large scale, iyokan bears large, slightly flattened orange fruit with an intensely fragrant rind and juicy, well-balanced sweet-tart flesh that is easy to peel by hand. Plant and care for it like other subtropical mandarin-type citrus, giving it full sun, steady moisture through fruit set, and protection from hard freezes, since it is less cold-tolerant than satsuma. Fruit ripens through the winter months and is one of the most widely eaten fresh citrus in Japan after satsuma mandarin. Its vigorous, moderately thorny growth benefits from light annual shaping to keep fruit within easy reach.
sources: University of California Riverside Citrus Variety Collection
Japan Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries citrus germplasm records

planting.note: Transplant after frost danger into full sun with excellent drainage; the very heavy fruit may need branch support as it sizes up.

directions: Named for the city of Hirado in Nagasaki Prefecture where it is a signature winter crop, this pomelo selection produces some of the largest edible citrus fruit grown, often a pound or more, with a thick pale rind and mild, sweet, low-bitterness flesh compared to typical pummelos. Give it a warm, sheltered full-sun site and generous root room, since the tree is vigorous and the fruit load is heavy enough to need sturdy limbs or staking support. Many growers cure picked fruit for a week or two at room temperature before eating, which softens the texture and rounds out the sweetness. It is a striking specimen tree for warm, frost-free gardens as well as a fruiting one.
sources: University of California Riverside Citrus Variety Collection
Japan Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries citrus germplasm records
